title: Budget Methodologies — Master, Flexible, ABB, ZBB & Project Budgets (CMA P1-B · feeds BAR)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — a job budget must speak the same language as actual cost

MBG structure: job cost codes roll into WIP GL accounts 1401 labor, 1402 materials, 1403 equipment, 1404 subcontractors, and 1405 other direct cost. A project budget built by phases and cost codes is useful only if JCS actuals map to the same definitions. Comparing a broad estimate category to differently classified actuals creates a variance that cannot guide action.

Budget methodology should fit the decision. A master budget coordinates the enterprise; a flexible budget separates volume from efficiency; activity-based budgeting estimates resource demand from activities; zero-based budgeting challenges discretionary spending; and a project budget controls a unique job across its lifecycle.

Master budget architecture

The master budget integrates operating and financial budgets. The sales or contract plan drives production or project activity, which drives labor, materials, subcontract, equipment, and overhead. Those budgets feed budgeted income, cash, and balance sheets. In construction, timing assumptions for draws, billings, retainage, vendor payments, and closings make the cash budget essential.

Schedules must articulate. Ending cash in the cash budget equals budgeted balance-sheet cash. Budgeted net income rolls into retained earnings. Capital spending affects cash and long-lived assets, with depreciation affecting income. Borrowing affects cash, debt, and interest. An assumption used in one schedule cannot silently differ elsewhere.

Static and flexible budgets

A static budget is based on planned activity. It is appropriate for planning but can be unfair for performance evaluation when actual volume differs. A flexible budget recalculates expected revenue and variable cost at actual activity while holding standards constant. The difference between actual results and flexible budget isolates price, efficiency, and spending effects; the difference between flexible and static budgets reflects activity volume.

Assume an illustrative project planned 100 framing units at $2,000 variable cost per unit plus $50,000 fixed site cost. Static budget is $250,000. Actual activity is 120 units, so flexible budget is 120 × $2,000 + $50,000 = $290,000. If actual cost is $310,000, the unfavorable spending/efficiency variance versus flexible budget is $20,000. Comparing actual to static budget would show $60,000 unfavorable and incorrectly attribute $40,000 of volume-related cost to performance.

Activity-based budgeting

Activity-based budgeting (ABB) forecasts activity demand from expected output, then estimates resources required. It reverses activity-based costing: first forecast jobs, change orders, purchase orders, inspections, or mobilizations; then multiply by resource consumption and rates.

Suppose illustratively procurement support costs $150 per purchase order and inspection support costs $400 per inspection. A job forecast of 80 POs and 15 inspections requires $12,000 + $6,000 = $18,000. A labor-hour-only budget could miss the support burden of a complex job. ABB is strongest when activity drivers are measurable and causally related; it becomes costly when every minor activity receives a pool.

Zero-based and incremental budgeting

Incremental budgeting starts with the current budget or actual and adjusts it. It is efficient for stable operations but perpetuates waste and outdated assumptions. Zero-based budgeting (ZBB) organizes discretionary work into decision packages, evaluates purpose and service level, and ranks funding from zero. ZBB does not mean every contractual or production cost is literally renegotiated from nothing each month.

An illustrative administrative software budget of $120,000 could be divided into required core licenses $70,000, enhanced analytics $30,000, and optional collaboration tools $20,000. Management ranks packages against objectives and risk rather than applying a blanket 5% cut. The analysis should include switching cost, control implications, and downstream labor—not price alone.

Project budgeting and cost-code control

A construction project budget begins with scope, quantities, production assumptions, unit rates, subcontract quotes, labor plan, equipment, permits, overhead policy, contingency, and schedule. Baseline changes require approved change control. Forecast at completion is distinct from original budget:

Forecast at completion = actual cost to date + current estimate to complete

Cost variance at completion = budget at completion − forecast at completion

Assume an illustrative job budget maps $100,000 labor to 1401, $250,000 materials to 1402, $50,000 equipment to 1403, $400,000 subcontractors to 1404, and $20,000 other direct cost to 1405. Total baseline is $820,000. Actual to date is $500,000 and current estimate to complete is $360,000, so forecast at completion is $860,000 and expected cost variance is $40,000 unfavorable.

Do not “fix” the original budget to equal the forecast. Preserve baseline, approved changes, current forecast, and actual separately. Otherwise management loses the history of estimating accuracy and scope decisions.

Contingency and change control

Contingency addresses identified uncertainty within defined scope; management reserve may address broader unknowns at a higher control level. Neither is revenue or profit. Define who can release contingency and how usage is documented.

A change order can affect contract price, budget, forecast, billing, and revenue recognition. Track proposed, submitted, approved, and rejected status. Do not add unapproved value to both contract price and project budget as if collection were certain. Scenario analysis can show outcomes while accounting follows supported terms.

Variance investigation

Set thresholds using amount, percentage, trend, risk, and controllability. A small recurring variance may reveal a broken standard; a large favorable variance may reflect missing invoices. Investigation should identify quantity, rate, mix, timing, classification, scope, and estimate changes.

Reconcile cost-code actuals to exact WIP GL control accounts before interpreting variance. A miscode between 1402 and 1404 changes category performance but not total WIP. A wrong entity changes both accountability and financial reporting.

Integrate the cash and balance-sheet budgets

A project cost budget does not reveal when cash leaves. Convert labor to payroll dates, materials to purchase and payment terms, subcontracts to progress payments and retainage, and overhead to recurring schedules. Align owner billings and draws with milestone, approval, and collection lags. The resulting cash schedule identifies financing needs before they become emergencies.

Budgeted WIP is a rollforward, not a percentage of revenue by default. Beginning WIP plus capitalizable job additions minus cost transferred on closings equals ending WIP. Budgeted AP follows received-but-unpaid costs, while retainage remains a separate obligation. Debt follows the loan schedule and interest calculation. These balance-sheet schedules must reconcile to the income and cash budgets.

Responsibility reporting should use the appropriate budget. A project manager can be evaluated against a flexible project budget and supported forecast; treasury against cash and financing; procurement against price, availability, and quality; finance against integration and forecast accuracy. Avoid assigning one undifferentiated total variance to a person who cannot control its drivers.

Document approved budget transfers. Moving dollars between codes can be legitimate after scope clarification, but it must not erase a cost overrun. Show original baseline, approved transfers, revised budget, actual, commitments, estimate to complete, and forecast at completion.

Worked example — the operating budget chain, schedule by schedule

The master budget is a chain in which each schedule feeds the next. Working it once with numbers is worth more than memorizing the diagram. All amounts are illustrative.

Production budget, in units

Budgeted sales are 12,000 units. Beginning finished-goods inventory is 1,500 units and the desired ending finished-goods inventory is 2,100 units.

Required production = budgeted sales + desired ending inventory − beginning inventory = 12,000 + 2,100 − 1,500 = 12,600 units.

Direct-materials purchases budget

Each unit requires 4 pounds, so production consumes 12,600 × 4 = 50,400 pounds. Beginning materials inventory is 6,000 pounds and desired ending materials inventory is 7,200 pounds.

Purchases = 50,400 + 7,200 − 6,000 = 51,600 pounds. At $3.50 per pound the purchases budget is 51,600 × $3.50 = $180,600.

Direct-labor budget

Each unit requires 1.5 hours, so 12,600 × 1.5 = 18,900 hours. At a $28 standard rate the labor budget is 18,900 × $28 = $529,200.

Cash collections schedule

Sales are $180,000 in January, $220,000 in February and $260,000 in March. MBG collects 50% in the month of sale, 35% in the following month and 15% in the second month after the sale.

March collections = (March sales × 50%) + (February sales × 35%) + (January sales × 15%) = $130,000 + $77,000 + $27,000 = $234,000.

Cash budget with a minimum balance

Beginning cash is $42,000, budgeted collections are the $234,000 above, and budgeted disbursements are $268,500. MBG must maintain a minimum cash balance of $30,000 and borrows in $1,000 increments to do so.

Cash available before financing = $42,000 + $234,000 − $268,500 = $7,500. The shortfall against the minimum is $30,000 − $7,500 = $22,500, which rounds up to $23,000 of borrowing. Ending cash is $7,500 + $23,000 = $30,500.

Trap — the inventory equation runs one way

Trap: in every quantity schedule the desired ending balance is added and the beginning balance is subtracted. Reversing them here gives 12,000 + 1,500 − 2,100 = 11,400 units, understating production by 1,200 units and cascading a 4,800-pound materials error and a 1,800-hour labor error into every downstream schedule. Reason it out rather than memorizing: you must build what you sell, plus what you want left over, less what you already have.

Trap — the borrowing increment

Trap: the answer is $30,500, not $30,000. Borrowing in $1,000 increments means the entity almost always ends slightly above its minimum. Answering with the minimum balance itself is the most common miss on this schedule type, and answering with the $22,500 shortfall confuses the borrowing need with the ending balance.

Trap — production units are not sales units

Trap: the materials and labor budgets key off the 12,600 production units, never the 12,000 budgeted sales units. Building materials off the sales figure understates purchases by 2,400 pounds and $8,400 before the ending-inventory adjustment is even considered.

Static, flexible and actual — the three-column discipline

Return to the illustrative job budgeted at $2,000 of variable cost per framing unit plus $50,000 of fixed site cost, planned at 100 units, with actual activity of 120 units and actual cost of $310,000.

ColumnCalculationAmount
Static budget (100 units)100 × $2,000 + $50,000$250,000
Flexible budget (120 units)120 × $2,000 + $50,000$290,000
Actual cost (120 units)Recorded$310,000
Activity variance$290,000 − $250,000$40,000, volume-driven
Spending/efficiency variance$310,000 − $290,000$20,000 unfavorable
Total static-budget variance$310,000 − $250,000$60,000 unfavorable

Only $20,000 of the $60,000 reflects performance. The other $40,000 is the cost of doing 20% more work, which is what the entity wanted.

Trap — flexing the fixed cost

Trap: the flexible budget flexes variable cost only. Fixed site cost stays at $50,000 whether activity is 100 or 120 units. Scaling the entire $250,000 static budget by the 20% activity increase gives $300,000 and a $10,000 unfavorable variance instead of $20,000 — a 50% understatement of the performance problem, produced by flexing $50,000 of cost that does not vary.

Worked example — why activity-based budgeting changes the answer

Compare two illustrative jobs that consume identical direct labor — 2,000 hours each — but differ sharply in transactional complexity. Support rates are $150 per purchase order and $400 per inspection.

DriverJob AJob B
Purchase orders80 × $150 = $12,000220 × $150 = $33,000
Inspections15 × $400 = $6,00042 × $400 = $16,800
Support cost required$18,000$49,800

Total support demand is $67,800. A labor-hour budget would spread that across 4,000 equal hours and assign $33,900 to each job — overstating Job A by $15,900 and understating Job B by $15,900. Job A appears unprofitable and Job B appears attractive, and the estimating team prices the next simple job too high and the next complex job too low.

Activity-based budgeting is not free. Each pool requires a driver that is measurable, causal, and worth tracking. Splitting a $67,800 support budget into fifteen pools to chase a few hundred dollars of accuracy costs more in data collection than the decision improvement is worth. Reserve it for drivers that materially change a pricing or resourcing decision.

Trap — a driver rate is a budget rate, not an actual

Trap: the $150 and $400 are budgeted rates from expected pool cost divided by expected driver volume. Charging jobs at actual pool cost divided by actual volume passes the support department's own spending and volume variances straight through to projects that could not influence either. Budget at standard, then account for the pool's spending variance where it can be managed.

Worked example — ranking zero-based decision packages

Return to the illustrative $120,000 administrative software budget, now expressed as ranked decision packages with a fourth candidate added.

RankDecision packageCostCumulativeFunded?
1Core licenses — required to operate$70,000$70,000Yes
2Automated bank feed — removes a manual control gap$18,000$88,000Yes
3Enhanced analytics$30,000$118,000Yes
4Optional collaboration tools$20,000$138,000No — exceeds the $120,000 cap

Ranking funds $118,000 of the $120,000 cap and consciously drops the lowest-value package. Contrast that with an across-the-board 5% cut applied to the three packages already inside the existing $120,000 budget, which sets it at $120,000 × 95% = $114,000 by shaving $3,500 from core licenses, $1,500 from analytics and $1,000 from collaboration — $6,000 in total. The core licenses cannot be bought at 95%, so the "cut" is fictional and reappears as an overrun. Across-the-board cuts protect the lowest-value spending and damage the highest-value spending, which is exactly the outcome ZBB exists to prevent.

Trap — ZBB does not rebuild contractual and production cost

Trap: zero-based budgeting challenges discretionary activities and service levels. It does not mean the subcontract schedule, payroll, debt service or committed lease costs are renegotiated from zero each cycle. Applying package ranking to committed obligations produces a budget the entity cannot legally execute, and it consumes the analytical effort that the genuinely discretionary $120,000 deserved.

Trap — a budget transfer is not a variance fix

Trap: in the $820,000 project baseline, moving $40,000 from account 1402 materials to 1404 subcontractors after a scope clarification is legitimate. Moving it to make an overrun disappear is not. The report must show original baseline, approved transfers, revised budget, actual, open commitments, estimate to complete and forecast at completion as separate columns — because the forecast at completion of $860,000 against a baseline of $820,000 is the number management needs, and any single "budget" column that has been quietly revised to $860,000 destroys it.

CPA Crossover — BAR

BAR tests budget integration, flexible-budget mechanics, driver-based forecasting, and variance interpretation. It may ask which budget changes with actual activity or why a favorable result is not necessarily good. Always identify the comparison basis before calculating a variance.

Practice and recap

  1. Select methodology based on the decision and cost behavior.
  2. Map budget lines to the same cost codes and GL controls used by actuals.
  3. Preserve baseline, approved changes, forecast, and actual separately.
  4. Flex variable cost for actual activity before judging performance.
  5. Use ABB for meaningful support drivers and ZBB for discretionary packages.
  6. Investigate missing, late, and misclassified costs before celebrating favorable variances.

Recap: no budget method is universally best. The master budget coordinates, the flexible budget normalizes volume, ABB models activity, ZBB challenges need, and the project budget controls scope and cost through a stable baseline and current forecast.

flashcards.back: A budget recalculated at actual activity using standard variable rates and expected fixed cost.
Activity demand, then resources and costs required for those activities.

flashcards.front: What is ZBB best suited to challenge?
flashcards.back: Discretionary activities and service levels through ranked decision packages.
Actual cost to date plus current estimate to complete.

flashcards.front: Why preserve the original project baseline?
flashcards.back: It retains accountability for estimating, scope changes, and forecast evolution.

flashcards.front: What WIP GL accounts receive the five job-cost categories?
flashcards.back: 1401 labor, 1402 materials, 1403 equipment, 1404 subcontractors, 1405 other direct.

flashcards.front: Why can a favorable cost variance be suspicious?
flashcards.back: It may reflect missing invoices, cutoff errors, or incomplete activity rather than efficiency.
The difference between flexible and static budgets caused by actual activity differing from planned activity.

questions.q: Illustrative variable cost is $2,000 per unit, fixed cost $50,000, and actual activity 120 units. Flexible budget is:
If actual cost is $310,000 and flexible budget $290,000, the variance is:
Which method starts by forecasting purchase orders and inspections?
questions.explain: ABB uses forecast activity drivers to estimate resource needs.

questions.q: Actual to date is $500,000 and estimate to complete $360,000. Forecast at completion is:
Budget at completion is $820,000 and forecast at completion $860,000. Expected cost variance is:
questions.explain: Forecast exceeds budget by $40,000, an unfavorable cost outlook.

questions.q: What is the main weakness of incremental budgeting?
choices: It can perpetuate waste and outdated assumptions
questions.explain: Starting from prior spending can embed activities that no longer support strategy.

questions.q: Why should baseline and forecast remain separate?
choices: To preserve original commitment and show current expected outcome
questions.explain: The baseline measures approved plan; the forecast updates expected results without rewriting history.
